title: Lake Zug lowered (Lorze outflow deepened)
place: Lake Zug; outflow of the Lorze at Cham
summary: The town of Zug deepened the Lorze river at Cham and lowered Lake Zug by about 2.5 m (1591–1592).
why: In the 16th century a road ran from Zug to Cham along the north shore of the lake. It crossed a marsh and was often flooded. The town of Zug decided to lower the lake to make the road safe from high water.

The town builder Jost Knopfli led the work. At the Obermühle in Cham, workers removed rock ribs and mill weirs that blocked the outflow. They also dug the river bed deeper over about 700 m. The work was finished in 1592. In the 1630s the outflow was deepened again.

Since then the mean lake level is about 2 to 2.5 m lower. A weir at Cham controls the outflow. The present weir dates from 1943. It can only change the lake level a little, because the Lorze can carry only a small amount of water.
gained: The lowering aimed to keep the road from Zug to Cham, which crossed a marsh on the north shore, safe from high water.
The lower lake level gave new land along the shore.
lost: Parts of the shore collapsed into the lake after the lowering.
The old mill weirs at the Obermühle in Cham were removed.

stops.title: A lower lake

stops.title: Lake Zug today
text: Today a weir at Cham, built in 1943, controls the outflow. In spring the level must not fall too low, because pike lay their eggs in the reeds.
In autumn the lake is kept low, so that the wet meadows near the shore can be mown.

notes: No shape: the lowering is older than all swisstopo maps (1844+), and no map shows the higher lake. Places checked by eye on today's map. Amount: HLS (Zugersee, Knopfli) says about 2.5 m; BAFU says the mean level is 'etwas mehr als zwei Meter' lower. HLS dates a second deepening to the 1630s; BAFU does not mention it. Gained/lost: HLS gives 'Landgewinne, aber auch Uferabbrüche' without places or sizes. The great shore collapses in the town of Zug (1435, 1887) are not linked to the lowering by the sources, so they are not used here. Lake regulation rules (pike spawning, mowing) are from BAFU.

title: Robenhuserriet: peat cutting at Lake Pfäffikon
place: Moors around Lake Pfäffikon, mainly the Robenhuserriet near Wetzikon and the Torfriet near Pfäffikon
built: Peat cutting from the early 18th century to the early 1950s; lake lowered in the 19th century; protected 1948
summary: For about 250 years people cut peat in the moors around Lake Pfäffikon; an artificial lowering of the lake in the 19th century let the shore moors grow, and in 1948 the canton protected the whole area.
why: Lake Pfäffikon lies in a basin left by the Rhine-Linth glacier. Large moors grew where the lake slowly filled up: the Robenhuserriet in the south and the Torfriet in the north.

Wood was short, so from the early 18th century people cut peat (dead plant material that burns) as fuel. Peat cutting competed for a long time with the cutting of litter (dry plants as bedding in stables). Peat was cut intensively in the early industrial age and in both world wars. It ended in the early 1950s.
In the 19th century the lake level was lowered artificially. The shore moors then spread over the former water area. In 1948 the canton of Zurich protected the whole area of Lake Pfäffikon.
gained: Peat gave fuel when wood was short. Much peat was cut at the start of industrialisation in the 19th century and in both world wars.
The lowering of the lake gave more room to the shore moors. Today the litter meadows of the Robenhuserriet are mown again, which keeps the wet habitats rich.
lost: Peat cutting removed large parts of the peat. The Torfriet is now a raised bog with regenerating areas, not an untouched one.
Part of the open lake was lost when the level was lowered.

title: Peat bogs of Les Ponts-de-Martel
place: Valley of La Sagne and Les Ponts, between Martel-Dernier, Les Ponts-de-Martel and Petit-Martel
built: Peat cutting from the 18th century; most in the two world wars
summary: For a long time people cut peat in the closed valley of Les Ponts-de-Martel; the largest raised bogs of Switzerland survive only as a small part of the old bog.
why: The valley of La Sagne and Les Ponts is a closed basin in the Jura. Its floor was once all marsh and raised bog (a moor fed only by rain, which grows up from peat moss).
Wood was short in the Jura, so people cut peat (dead plant material that burns) as fuel. In both world wars the marsh was used for peat again.

Peat cutting fell sharply after 1945, and the Rothenthurm vote of 1987 banned it in Switzerland. Since 1991 the Marais Rouge has been in the federal inventory of raised bogs, and the valley is a moor landscape of national importance since 1996. The canton now makes cut bogs wet again.
gained: The marsh gave peat, most of all in the two world wars, when coal was rationed.
Drained peat land became meadows and fields. Today some fairly intensive crops grow on former peat bogs.
lost: Large parts of the raised bogs were cut for peat. About 130 ha of raised bog remain, still the largest in Switzerland.
Most remaining raised bogs show traces of peat cutting: bare surfaces, old cutting pits and long, straight peat banks.

title: Baldeggersee lowered
place: Baldeggersee in the Seetal, between Hochdorf and Richensee
summary: The Baldeggersee was lowered in 1806 and again in 1870–1871, by about 1.5 m in all, to win farmland at its flat north and south ends.
why: Before the lowering the lake was clearly longer. In the north it reached the walls of the small town of Richensee. In the south it reached almost to Hochdorf.

To gain farmland, people lowered the lake in 1806 and again in 1870–1871. In all the level fell by about 1.5 m. In 1871 alone it fell by 75 to 90 cm. Wide areas of shallow water at the north and south ends became dry.
Today the lake is 4.5 km long. Its shores have long reed belts, and important wetlands lie at both ends.
gained: New farmland at the flat north and south ends of the lake.
For many years after 1871, lapwings and curlews bred on the new wet land in the south, between Urswil and Hochdorf.
lost: Wide shallow and slightly marshy areas at both ends of the lake became dry.
Rich hunting grounds for water birds disappeared, according to a local bird observer (1942).

stops.title: Lowered twice

This map sheet was first drawn earlier, but its shore fits today's lake (blue). So it cannot show the older, larger lake, and no old shore is drawn.

stops.title: Baldeggersee today
text: Today the lake is 4.5 km long. Long reed belts grow between the water and the farmland.
The lake suffered from too many nutrients for decades. Since the early 1980s air is pumped into it.

notes: No old shore: the Dufour map (shown for 1865 and still in 1895) has the same outline as today's lake within the map accuracy (checked by overlay of the OSM lake), so it does not show the lake before 1806 and cannot show a clear difference for 1871. The lake height on the Dufour sheet is printed '467' (1865) and '466.4' (later edition, 1895); this may reflect the 1871 lowering, but the map heights use an older reference level, so I did not use it as evidence. After: Baldeggersee from OpenStreetMap, checked by eye. Facts: BLN sheet 1304 (BAFU 2017: 1806 and 1870, about 1.5 m in all; lake reached Richensee and nearly Hochdorf); J. Bussmann, Ornithologischer Beobachter 39 (1942): lowering in spring and summer 1871 by 75-90 cm, birds. Year conflict: BLN 1870, Bussmann 1871; I wrote 1870–1871. The HLS article (Baldeggersee) has no data on the lowering.

title: Lake Sempach lowered
place: Lake Sempach (Sempachersee), between Sursee and Sempach
summary: In 1806 Lake Sempach was lowered by about 1.8 m to win farmland; the lower water exposed prehistoric lakeshore settlements.
why: The level of Lake Sempach often changed. People lowered the lake on purpose already in 1479 and around 1760. Later the water rose again.
In 1806 the lake was lowered by about 1.8 m to gain land. Other sources give 1.5 to 2 m.

The lower water uncovered prehistoric lakeshore settlements (villages of wooden houses on posts near the water). People collected many finds already in 1806. These sites have been exposed to erosion since then.
gained: The lowering gave new land along the shore for farming.
People collected many old objects on the dry shore. These are the first reported finds of prehistoric wetland settlements in the canton of Lucerne.
lost: The prehistoric settlements lost their protective water cover. Since 1806 waves wear them away. Today many sites are in very poor condition, and in places only the tips of the posts remain.
On the west shore the old sites now lie on dry land, and building, drains and farming damaged some of them.

title: Wauwilermoos: a lake and a moor drained
place: Wauwil plain between Egolzwil, Wauwil, Schötz and Kottwil
built: 1853–1856 (lake drained); peat cutting from about 1820; drainage works mainly 1940s
summary: Lucerne drained the last part of the Wauwilersee in 1853–1856; later peat cutting and drainage turned the surrounding moor into farmland.
why: The Wauwil plain lies in a basin left by the Reuss glacier. Around 1800 a lake of about 70 ha lay there, in a large moor (a wet area where peat forms). The villages around it made the lake smaller step by step.

In 1836 the canton of Lucerne bought the lake back. In 1853–1856 the canton drained the last 20 ha of the lake. People cut peat (dead plant material that burns) for fuel from about 1820. Most peat was cut during the two world wars and when the Ron stream was corrected in 1940–1943.

In the Second World War the Wahlen plan (the 'cultivation battle', to grow more food at home) pushed drainage further. Interned foreign soldiers did much of the work. Today the plain is intensive farmland. Only a reserve of 16 ha remains wet.
gained: The drained plain became farmland. Today it is used intensively for farming.
Peat gave fuel, mainly in the two world wars when coal was short.
After the drainage, Stone Age settlements came to light on the old shore. They are important finds for archaeology.
lost: The lake and almost all of the moor disappeared. The Great Curlew and the Common Snipe stopped breeding in the plain.
Peat was cut several metres deep and the drained soil sank. After the drainage works of the Second World War, about 34 ha could not be fully farmed any more.
A bird reserve set up in 1926 was ploughed for potatoes and oats during the war. Only a strip of 3 ha was protected again in 1958.

title: Flon and Louve in Lausanne
place: Lausanne, from La Sallaz through the town centre and Sévelin to the lake at Vidy
summary: Lausanne put its two town rivers, the Flon and the Louve, into vaults and filled their valleys; the town centre now stands on top of them.
why: The Flon and the Louve cut deep valleys through Lausanne. The town wanted to grow and to cross these valleys. It also wanted protection from floods and cleaner streets, after the cholera epidemic that hit Europe in 1832.

The town began to vault (cover with an arch) the Flon in the Rôtillon quarter in 1836 and the Louve at the Place de la Riponne in 1840. The work went on in stages. By 1873 both rivers had disappeared from the townscape. Their valleys were partly filled in.

West of the town the Flon stayed open for longer. The maps show that it was covered in stages after 1925. In 1964 the last part, in the Vallée de la Jeunesse, disappeared for the national exhibition. Today the vaults carry waste water. The clean water of the two rivers is led away before it reaches them.
gained: Large flat building land in the steep town. Part of the town grew on the filled valleys of the Flon and the Louve.
Better hygiene and flood protection: the city names both reasons for the first vaults.
lost: About 9 km of rivers now flow underground in the town. The vaults lie deep: the Flon vault is 17 to 22 m below the ground at Sévelin.
The city says that opening the Flon and the Louve again is impossible. It can only mark their old course on the surface.

title: Sionne in Sion
place: Sion, from the north edge of the town along the Rue du Grand-Pont to the south-east of the old town
summary: Sion vaulted the Sionne under its main street, the Grand-Pont, around 1848; the stretch just north of the old town followed between 1960 and 1980.
why: The Sionne comes down from the mountains north of Sion and flows through the town to the Rhône. For centuries it ran open along the main street, the Grand-Pont, and it also supplied the town with water. The town hall was built on the Grand-Pont in 1657–1665.

Around 1848 the town vaulted (covered with an arch) the whole stretch in the old town. This made it easier to pass along the Grand-Pont, and the streets were made wider. In the same years the town tore down its walls and laid out new squares.

North of the old town the stream stayed open for another century. The maps show it open in 1960 and covered in 1980, when the area was built over. Today the Sionne is open again only above this stretch and below the old town.
gained: An easier passage and wider streets in the old town along the Grand-Pont.
More room for streets and houses north of the old town: the map of 1980 shows this area built over the covered stream.
lost: The open stream in the main street of the old town disappeared around 1848.
About 650 m of open stream north of the old town were covered between 1960 and 1980 (seen and measured on the maps).

title: The loss of Swiss moors and wetlands
place: All of Switzerland, mainly the Central Plateau, the Jura and the Prealps
built: Mainly 1850–1950; about 80,000 ha drained 1885–1940 and 80,000 ha more in the Second World War
summary: Since about 1800, Switzerland has lost about 90% of its moors and wetlands to drainage, peat cutting and farming; in 1987 the people voted to protect the rest.
why: Around 1700, wetlands and moors covered about 5% of today's Switzerland. People used them for litter (dry plants as bedding in stables), hay and peat (dead plant material that burns), which replaced firewood. Peat was first used as fuel in Zurich and Neuchâtel in the early 18th century. In the 19th century peat was cut in almost all raised bogs of the Plateau and the Jura.

From the 19th century, common land was divided and wet land was drained to grow more food. From 1885 to 1940 about 80,000 ha were drained with clay pipes and other methods. In the Second World War the 'cultivation battle' (the Wahlen plan, to grow more food at home) added another 80,000 ha.

After 1950 peat and litter lost their importance. A federal law on nature protection came in 1966. In December 1987 people and cantons accepted the Rothenthurm initiative, which protects all moors and moor landscapes of national importance and also banned peat cutting.
gained: Large areas of new farmland. Between 1885 and 1940 about 80,000 ha of moor were drained, and in the Second World War about 80,000 ha more.
Peat gave fuel when wood and coal were short.
Since 1987 the remaining moors of national importance have strong protection in the Federal Constitution.
lost: By the start of the 21st century the moors had shrunk by about 90%, to about 0.5% of the country's area.
Moors are the main habitat of many protected plants and animals, such as sundew and cotton grass. Most of this habitat is gone.
Even protected moors are still threatened by continued drainage and by nutrients from farming.

stops.title: A country with many wet places
text: In the 19th century many valley floors and plains were still wet. Old maps show them with blue dashes (marsh symbols).
People cut litter and peat there, but they also wanted more land for crops.

stops.title: Drained for food
text: From 1885 to 1940 about 80,000 ha were drained. In the Second World War another 80,000 ha followed, to grow more food at home.

stops.title: A protected rest
text: Today moors cover only about 0.5% of Switzerland. The vote of 1987 protects the moors of national importance.

title: Lake Lucerne regulated by the Reuss needle weir
place: Outflow of the Reuss from Lake Lucerne, city of Lucerne
summary: A movable needle weir in the Reuss at Lucerne replaced the old fixed sills and has regulated the level of Lake Lucerne since 1861.
why: Since the 13th century, mills in Lucerne used sills (low walls across the river) in the Reuss. Each new sill raised the river and the lake a little more. This helped ships, but the shores up to Flüelen and Alpnachstad flooded more often. After each flood the lake cantons complained to Lucerne.

In 1858 the lake cantons and the Centralbahn railway company signed a contract, with the federal government taking part. From 1859 to 1861 a movable needle weir replaced the fixed sill. A needle weir is a row of wooden boards (needles) that workers put in or take out by hand. Rules for the weir followed in 1867. Since then the lake has been kept at a much lower level than before.

The weir still could not carry the largest floods, for example in 1910 and 2005. From 2009 to 2011 it was rebuilt. The outflow at high water grew by about a quarter. New rules let the level move as in a natural lake within a narrow band, which helps the wetlands on the shore.
gained: The lake level could be held much lower than before, so the shores flooded less often.
The rebuilt weir (2011) lets more water out at high water, by about a quarter.
lost: Floods still reached the lake shores, for example in 1910 and 2005.
Changes of the lake level have a large effect on the plants and animals of the shore. The rules of 2011 let the level move as in a natural lake within a narrow band.

title: Grande Cariçaie: a marsh made by lowering the lake
place: South-east shore of Lake Neuchâtel, from Yverdon to the Thielle canal
built: Lake lowered by the first Jura water correction (1868–1891); shore marshes grew from about 1880
summary: When the first Jura water correction lowered Lake Neuchâtel, a sand strip several hundred metres wide fell dry on the south shore; it was not farmed, and it became the largest lake-shore marsh of Switzerland.
why: The first Jura water correction (1868–1891) lowered and linked the three lakes at the foot of the Jura, to stop floods in the Seeland (see the change 'jura'). The lowering changed the shores deeply.

In many places people used the new land for farms, workshops, roads and houses. On the gently sloping south-east shore of Lake Neuchâtel this did not happen. There the lower water freed a band of sand several hundred metres wide. Plants and animals took it over quickly.
In 1982 Vaud and Fribourg adopted a joint plan to manage the shore. Today it is a nature reserve, a moor landscape of national importance and a Ramsar site (wetland of international importance).
gained: The largest natural marshy lake shore of Switzerland: about 40 km long, with more than 3000 ha in the reserve.
It is the most important breeding site in Switzerland for water birds and waders, with many rare and threatened species.
The lower water also uncovered pile-dwelling sites along the lake shores, which are of great value for archaeology.
lost: The old shore line and its open water disappeared; villages and old harbours that were on the water's edge moved away from the lake.
Without care, the marshes and floodplain forests slowly dry out and change into forest. They now need regular management.

title: Albisrieder Dorfbach and Zurich's stream plan
place: Zurich, between Albisrieden and Altstetten
built: piped between 1880 and 1960; partly opened again after 1988
length_km: c. 1.4 (drawn old course); c. 1 open again
summary: Like most streams in Zurich, the Albisrieder Dorfbach disappeared into a pipe as the town grew; since the city's stream plan of 1988, about 1 km of it flows open again.
why: Around 1850 about 160 km of open streams ran through the area of today's city of Zurich. As the town grew fast, the streams were seen as an obstacle. In rain they carried gravel and caused floods. So many streams were straightened or put into pipes (eingedolt). By 1980 only about 60 km were still open, most of them in the forest. Across Switzerland, about a quarter of all stream stretches are artificial, heavily changed or piped today.

The Albisrieder Dorfbach is one example. On the map of 1880 it flowed through wet meadows from Albisrieden to Altstetten. On the map of 1960 the stream is gone: the area was built over and the water ran in a pipe.

In 1988 the city adopted a stream plan (Bachkonzept). Its aim is to open piped streams wherever possible. Clean stream water should flow on the surface and not go into the sewers and the treatment plant. Outside the forests, open streams grew from 16 km in 1988 to 34 km. The Albisrieder Dorfbach is one of the streams the city names: it now flows open again through green spaces.
gained: The land over the piped stream could be built over, as the map of 1960 shows. The city names two reasons for piping streams: they were an obstacle to the growing town, and in rain they brought gravel and floods.

Since the stream was opened again, clean water no longer goes into the sewers without need. The city says that open streams give back living space to plants and animals and make the quarters more pleasant.
lost: The map of 1880 shows the stream and its wet meadows (Bachwiesen) between Albisrieden and Altstetten. The maps of 1960 and 1985 show no stream there.
The maps show that the new open stream does not follow its old bed: it runs about 50 to 80 m further east, between new buildings.

title: Zurich lake quays (Quaianlagen)
place: Lower end of Lake Zurich, city of Zurich (Enge, Zurich, Riesbach)
summary: Zurich, Enge and Riesbach filled in the lower end of Lake Zurich and built a continuous quay with parks and the Quaibrücke bridge (1881–1887).
why: Before the 1880s the city of Zurich touched the lake only for a short distance. The shores in Enge and Riesbach were rural. In 1863 the canton fixed new shore lines further out in the lake, to allow a continuous quay road.

In 1871 the canton planned a railway along the shore of the lower lake basin. The communes of Zurich, Enge and Riesbach feared they would lose their shore. They fought the plan together and built quays instead. The engineer Arnold Bürkli led the work. Earth was filled into the lake, and the Quaibrücke bridge (1882–1884) joined the two shores.

The quays opened in 1887. They run from the Enge harbour to the Riesbach harbour. The Arboretum park and the Seefeldquai were laid out on the new land. The city later extended the quays, until the 1960s.
gained: The city gained a continuous lake promenade with avenues, lawns and parks, among them the Arboretum.
The Quaibrücke bridge (1882–1884) crosses the Limmat where it leaves the lake. It joined the quays of both shores into one promenade.
lost: About 26 ha of shallow lake were filled in (measured on the maps). A post that marked Zurich's fishing rights stood about 100 m from the shore. Today it stands in the park.
The old shore line disappeared under the fill. At the Utoquai and the Seefeldquai the new shore is a quay wall.

title: Lake Geneva regulated at the Rhône outflow in Geneva
place: Outflow of the Rhône from Lake Geneva, city of Geneva
summary: After a seven-year court case, Geneva, Vaud and Valais agreed in 1884 to regulate Lake Geneva at its outflow; a weir at the Pont de la Machine and, since 1995, the Seujet dam keep the level within 60 cm.
why: The level of Lake Geneva always changed strongly with the seasons. From 1877 to 1884 a court case about the lake level ran before the Federal Court.

On 17 December 1884 Geneva, Vaud and Valais signed a convention. Its main aim was to let more water flow out of the lake, so that high levels would be lower. From 1883 to 1888 Geneva built works in the Rhône, among them a regulating weir at the Pont de la Machine. Rules for the weir followed in 1892.

In 1984 a new act decided to replace the old works with the Seujet dam, which also makes electricity. It opened in 1995. The level must stay between 371.70 m and 372.30 m above sea level, as under the rules of 1884.
gained: A steady lake level. Every winter the level is lowered, so the lake can take in the snow melt in spring without flooding the shores.
In leap years the level is lowered more in spring, so that the shores can be cleaned and harbours and shore walls repaired.
The Seujet dam also makes electricity from the Rhône.
lost: The natural rise and fall of the lake with the seasons ended. The lake now follows a fixed yearly pattern set by the cantons.

title: Birsig in Basel
place: Old town of Basel, from the Heuwaage to the Rhine at the Schifflände
summary: Basel covered its town stream, the Birsig, in stages: the part under the Falknerstrasse around 1900 and the part from the Heuwaage to the Barfüsserplatz in the 1950s.
why: The Birsig flows through the middle of old Basel to the Rhine. For centuries it was the main sewer (cloaca maxima) of the town. Toilets at the back of the houses dropped waste straight into the stream. The water was often too low to wash the waste away.

Voters said no to a sewer law and to the clean-up of the Birsig in 1876 and 1881. In 1896 they accepted a sewer system. In 1898 the Great Council decided to put the stretch between the Barfüsserplatz and the main post office underground. The new Falknerstrasse was built on top. The part near the Marktplatz was covered around 1886–1890.

The stretch from the Heuwaage to the Barfüsserplatz stayed open until the 1950s. Then it was covered too, and the space became a car park. Today the Birsig is open only upstream of the Heuwaage, near the zoo. A citizens' initiative asks for a more open Birsig, and the city plans light pavilions over the covered stream.
gained: The town got rid of an open sewer in its centre. The covering went together with the new sewer system.
A new street, the Falknerstrasse, was built on the covered bed around 1900. In the 1950s a car park was made over the next stretch.
lost: The Birsig disappeared from the townscape. The old back houses along the stream were pulled down soon after the new street was built.
The covering must be maintained: in 1999 the city had to repair the hundred-year-old vault under the Falknerstrasse.

summary: The wild Krienbach once flowed open along the Obergrundstrasse into Lucerne; it was covered in the 19th and 20th centuries, and since 1993 a tunnel takes its floods to the Reuss.
why: The Krienbach comes down from the north side of the Pilatus through Kriens to Lucerne. It carried much gravel and caused many heavy floods, for example in 1343, 1473, 1566 and, very badly, in 1738. From the 15th century the town had a special officer who watched over the stream.

In the 19th and 20th centuries most of the stream in the town was covered. The building of the tramway around 1900 was one reason. The maps show the stream open along the Obergrundstrasse in 1890 and 1912, and mostly gone by 1940.
The pipe did not end the floods. After the flood of 1988, the stream was led through a tunnel under the Sonnenberg hill into the Reuss. This tunnel was finished in 1993.
gained: Room for the street and the tramway into the Obergrund quarter, built around 1900.
Since 1993 the tunnel under the Sonnenberg protects the town from the floods of the Krienbach.
lost: The Krienbach disappeared from the townscape of the Obergrund quarter.
The covered stream could still flood the town, as it did in 1988.

title: Neeracher Ried: the last part of a large fen
place: Lower Glatt valley between Neerach, Höri, Niederhasli and Steinmaur
built: Drains 1891; peat cutting until 1928; most of the Ried drained after the 1930s; full melioration 1968–1976
summary: Until the 1930s a fen of 3–4 km² lay between Neerach, Höri, Niederhasli and Steinmaur; drainage turned most of it into farmland, and only three reserves remain.
why: Moraines close the valley to the north, so water collects in the basin of Neerach. A large fen (a wet meadow on peat soil, fed by ground water) grew there. In 1891 drains and irrigation channels were built in the Neeracher Ried.
The communes leased the use of the Ried: litter and hay, ice for breweries, peat cutting until 1928, and even the right to catch frogs until 1949.

Until the 1930s the Ried still covered 3–4 km². Later most of it was drained for farming; a full melioration (drainage and land consolidation) of Neerach followed in 1968–1976. The bird protection society has protected a core since 1927, and the canton since 1956.
gained: Most of the former Ried became farmland around the reserves. A large land improvement (Gesamtmelioration) followed in 1968–1976.
Litter, hay, ice and peat for the villages, as long as the Ried was used in the old way.
lost: Most of the 3–4 km² of Ried. Only the Neeracher Ried (103 ha), the Steinmaurer Ried (12 ha) and the Neerer See (15 ha) remained.
Breeding birds such as the Whinchat (until 1964) and the Great Reed Warbler (until 1979) disappeared from the reserve.

title: Nant de Couchefatte (Chancy)
place: Chancy and Avully, from the Passeiry plateau to the Rhône at the Chancy-Pougny power plant
length_km: c. 1.5 (drawn old course); c. 1 open again
summary: A small country stream near Chancy was put in a pipe over most of its length in the 20th century; from 2005 the canton opened it again in stages, also to protect the Chancy-Pougny power plant from floods.
why: The Nant de Couchefatte is a small stream of 2.6 km. It rises on the Passeiry plateau and flows into the Rhône at the Chancy-Pougny hydropower plant. On the map of 1900 it flowed open past the mill of Moulin Roget and the hamlet of Le Martinet.
Later most of the stream was put in a pipe (mis sous tuyau). The maps of 1960, 1995 and 2010 show no open stream here. The sources do not say when or why it was piped.

Geneva has had a programme to restore its streams since 1997. Here the aims were to protect the power plant from floods and to open the stream again. A first stage with a flood basin at Moulin Roget was built in 2005, a second stage upstream to Le Martinet in 2006–2007, and a third stage was planned for 2011.
gained: Since 2005: protection of the Chancy-Pougny power plant from floods, a flood basin at Moulin Roget, and an open stream again. The canton reports trout breeding in the lower part.
lost: For decades most of the stream ran in a pipe. In 2011 the canton still described it as piped over most of its length.
The waste water of the hamlet of Passeiry first had to be connected to the treatment plant of Chancy (2007), so that the open stream stays clean.

title: Lac de Joux and Lac Brenet regulated for the La Dernier power station
place: Vallée de Joux: Lac de Joux and Lac Brenet; power station La Dernier near Vallorbe
built: 1901–1904; Lac Brenet held lower later (by about 1960)
summary: From 1901 a power company regulated the two lakes of the Vallée de Joux through a tunnel to the La Dernier power station; later the small Lac Brenet was held lower, and its west end became pasture.
why: The lakes of the Vallée de Joux have no river outflow. Their water sinks into holes in the limestone (karst) and comes out again as the source of the Orbe. When the holes could not take enough water, the lake level rose and flooded the valley.

In 1901 the canton gave a concession to the company Forces Motrices de Joux et Brenet. Its aim was to stop the large changes of the lake level. From 1901 to 1904 a tunnel was built from the lakes to a pressure pipe above Vallorbe. The La Dernier power station uses the lake water to make electricity and to regulate the level.

In long dry periods the two lakes stopped flowing into each other, and costly pumps were needed. So new rules followed. Lac Brenet was held at about 1002 m. Gates on the canal between the lakes made Lac de Joux a storage basin (up to 1005 m).
gained: The tunnel to La Dernier made the valley safe from floods if the natural holes became blocked.
The La Dernier power station uses the lake water to regulate the level and to make electricity.
The lower Lac Brenet gave the village of Les Charbonnières new pasture land.
lost: The level of the lakes now depends on the power station. In 2011, turbines lowered Lac de Joux by 25 cm for repair work, during a dry spring.
Part of Lac Brenet fell dry at its west and south ends. Measured on the swisstopo map of 1955 and on OpenStreetMap, the lake shrank from about 85 ha to about 65 ha.

title: Klöntalersee (Löntsch power plant)
place: Klöntal west of Glarus, dam at Rhodannenberg
summary: An earth dam at the east end of the natural Klöntalersee raised the lake for the Löntsch power plant; the lake grew much larger and covered the flat valley floor to the west.
why: The Klöntal is a side valley of the Linth valley near Glarus. It already had a natural lake. West of the lake, the Klönbach flowed through a flat valley floor near Vorauen.

From 1905 to 1908 the company that later became the NOK (today Axpo) built the Löntsch power plant. An earth dam at Rhodannenberg, at the east end of the lake, raised the water. The lake became a seasonal store. A pipeline takes the water down to the power station near Netstal, 372 m lower.
The power station is called the birthplace of Axpo. The dam was renewed from 1971 to 1975, and the power station in 2016.
gained: The power station makes about 119 GWh of electricity per year from the water of an 83 km² catchment.
The lake now stores about 40 million m³ of usable water. Today the Klöntal is a popular area for recreation.
lost: The lake grew a lot, says HLS. The maps of 1904 and today show that it flooded the flat valley floor west of the old lake, where the Klönbach flowed.

title: Eulach at Winterthur station
place: Winterthur, from the south-west corner of the old town (Untertor) past the station to the Schützenwiese
summary: The Eulach once flowed open past the old town gate and the station square of Winterthur; between 1910 and 1940 this stretch disappeared under the ground.
why: The Eulach flows through Winterthur to the Töss. For centuries it drove mills beside the old town: around 1480 six mills stood on the Eulach. The Untertor quarter, at the west end of the old town, grew along the stream.
The railway came in 1855. The town walls disappeared, and the station square became a traffic hub. In 1895 a writer still described the noise of the open Eulach near the station square.

The maps show the stream open past the Untertor and under the railway in 1910. On the map of 1940 this stretch is gone. No source found says why or exactly when it was covered. Today nothing of the Eulach can be seen on the station square.
lost: The open stream near the station square disappeared. A writer still described it there in 1895. The maps show it open in 1910 and gone in 1940.

title: Rothenthurm moor: peat cutting, an army plan and a vote
place: High valley of the Biber between Rothenthurm and Biberbrugg
built: Peat cutting from the 18th century, most in the two world wars; protected after the vote of 1987
summary: People cut peat in the Rothenthurm moor for fuel for two centuries; when the army planned a training ground there, a federal vote in 1987 protected all Swiss moors of national importance.
why: The Rothenthurm high valley has one of the largest moor landscapes of Switzerland. Raised bogs (moors fed only by rain, which grow up from peat moss over thousands of years) cover large parts of it.

In the 18th century Switzerland had lost much of its forest, and wood was short. People began to dig peat (dead plant material that burns) as fuel. In the world wars peat cutting became an industry. In Rothenthurm up to 500 workers and peat machines worked in the peat fields. Until the Second World War many people in the village lived partly from peat.

In the 1970s and 1980s the federal government planned an army training ground in the moor. By then most Swiss moors were already gone. A people's initiative asked to protect all moors and moor landscapes of national importance without conditions. People and cantons accepted it in December 1987. The training ground was not built, and peat cutting was banned.
gained: Peat gave fuel in times of need, when wood was short. In the world wars up to 500 workers cut peat in the Rothenthurm peat fields.
The vote of 1987 gave strong protection in the Federal Constitution to all moors and moor landscapes of national importance in Switzerland, not only Rothenthurm.
The moor landscape (1138 ha) is now protected. It also gives drinking water to four Zurich communes, about two million cubic metres each year.
lost: Peat cutting removed parts of the raised bogs. Old peat cutting edges and small peat huts still show where peat was dug.
Raised bogs grow very slowly, so cut peat does not come back in human time. Today projects make some cut bogs wet again (bog regeneration).
Across Switzerland, about 90% of the raised bogs disappeared, mainly by drainage and peat cutting.

title: Aare (Wohlensee reservoir)
place: Aare between Bern and Mühleberg
summary: The Mühleberg dam held back the Aare west of Bern over 12 km; the river became the long, winding Wohlensee.
why: West of Bern, the Aare wound in loops through a deep valley. Farms stood on the low land beside the river. A ferry crossed the river at Wohlei.
From 1917 to 1921 the Bernische Kraftwerke (BKW) built the Mühleberg hydropower plant near Niederruntigen. The dam held back the Aare over a length of 12 km. The Wohlensee was born in 1920.
Today the lake is an important protected area for animals and plants. It is also used for water sports near Bern, mostly rowing.
gained: The commune of Wohlen got new roads and bridges and tax income. A new bridge at Kappelen and the Wohlei bridge were built. The Wohlei bridge replaced a ferry.
The lake became an important protected area for fauna and flora, and a place for rowing near Bern.
lost: Several farms had to be given up.
The commune of Wohlen lost farmland and several dozen houses. The old covered wooden bridge at Kappelen was replaced.

title: Lago Ritom (raised natural lake)
place: Piora plateau above Piotta, Leventina
summary: The Swiss railways dammed the natural Lago Ritom and raised it by about 22 m, to make electricity for the Gotthard line.
why: Lago Ritom is a natural lake on the Piora plateau, high above the Leventina valley. In 1916 the map shows it at about 1830 m, with the delta of the Murinascia stream and the alp of Campo at its east end.

The Swiss Federal Railways wanted to run the Gotthard line with electricity. They built a dam at the outlet of the lake in 1917 and a power station at Piotta below. The HLS lists Ritom (1920) and Amsteg (1922) as power plants built by the railways.

The dam raised the lake from 1828 m to a highest level of 1850 m. The higher lake flooded the delta of the Murinascia Grande. A new pumped-storage plant of Ritom SA, owned by the railways and the canton, has been built since 2018.
gained: The lake gave the railways their own electricity for the Gotthard line from about 1920.
A new pumped-storage plant (work started in 2018, about 250 million francs) replaces the old plant of 1917. Pumped storage means water can also be pumped back up to the lake.
lost: The higher lake flooded the delta of the Murinascia Grande and the flat land at its east end, near the alp of Campo.

title: Jogne (Lac de Montsalvens)
place: Lower Jogne valley between Charmey and Broc
summary: One of the first arch dams in Europe closed the Jogne valley above Broc in 1921 to end a shortage of electricity in the canton of Fribourg.
why: Between Charmey and Broc the Jogne flowed through a valley with scattered buildings, before it entered a gorge above Broc.

The canton lacked electricity. In 1918 the Fribourg parliament ordered a dam by decree. A concrete arch dam 52 m high was built at the entrance of the gorge from 1919 to 1921. It is one of the first arch dams in Europe. It was raised in 1926 to produce more.
The water drives the Broc power station of the Fribourg power company (today Groupe E). The left abutment was strengthened in 1997–1998.
gained: The lake holds about 12 million m³ of water for the Broc power station (30 MW).
The dam was raised in 1926 to increase production.
lost: The lake covers about 1 km² of the Jogne valley floor. The map of 1918 shows buildings there, for example at Saudy and Praz Paufert.

title: Hudelmoos: the last raised bog of Thurgau
place: Shallow basin between Zihlschlacht, Hagenwil and Muolen
built: Peat cutting until about the 1950s; edges drained until 1962; protected 1977
summary: The Hudelmoos once covered at least 1 km²; peat cutting and drainage of its edges left a strongly cut raised bog of about 25 ha, the only partly preserved raised bog in canton Thurgau.
why: The Hudelmoos lies in a shallow basin between Zihlschlacht and Hagenwil. It was a raised bog (a moor fed only by rain, which grows up from peat moss). A bird study of 1988 estimates that it first covered at least 1 km².

People cut peat (dead plant material that burns) and litter there. About 1928 there were still 50 ha of open Ried. Until 1962 another 25 ha at the edges were drained and turned into farmland or spruce plantations.
Peat cutting stopped about 30 years before 1988. St. Gallen and Thurgau protected the rest in 1977. Two ponds were made in 1973 and 1978 to replace the old peat pits, which had filled up.
gained: The moor gave peat and litter (cut marsh plants used as bedding in stables).
New farmland and spruce forest at the edges of the moor: until 1962, 25 ha more were drained there.
lost: Most of the bog. The rest of about 25 ha is a strongly cut raised bog, with fens, transition mires and heath.
After litter cutting stopped in the 1950s, birch woods grew on the Thurgau side, and spruce spread from the plantations.
The Common Snipe stopped breeding there. The Marsh Clubmoss, still present about 1938, has disappeared.

title: Rhine at Eglisau (Eglisau power plant)
place: Rhine between Eglisau and Rheinsfelden (Glattfelden)
summary: A power plant at Rheinsfelden raised the Rhine at Eglisau by 8 m in 1920; 30 houses and the old wooden bridge of the little bridge town were pulled down.
why: Eglisau is an old bridge town on the Rhine. A wooden bridge crossed the river there, and houses stood low at the water's edge.

Below the Rhine Falls, nine power plants were built on the Rhine from 1898. One of them is the Eglisau plant at Rheinsfelden, in the commune of Glattfelden. It was finished in 1920. In that year the plant held back the Rhine and raised it by 8 m at Eglisau.
Because the water would rise, 30 houses and the wooden bridge were pulled down. In 1919 a new concrete bridge with three arches replaced the old bridge.
gained: The power plant makes electricity from the Rhine. The dam list gives a weir of 20 m and a held-back volume of about 7 million m³.
Eglisau got a new concrete bridge in 1919.
lost: 30 houses and the old wooden bridge were pulled down.
The fast-flowing Rhine at Eglisau became a calm, held-back river. HLS says that living conditions changed in such reservoirs with weak current.

title: Barberine (Lac d'Emosson)
place: Barberine plateau above Finhaut, on the border with France
summary: The Swiss railways dammed the Barberine plateau in 1925 for electric trains; the much larger Emosson dam of the 1970s drowned the old dam and the plateau.
why: Above Finhaut the Barberine stream flowed over a flat high plateau with a small hamlet and alp huts. During the First World War coal became scarce and expensive. The Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) wanted their own electricity to run electric trains.

The SBB got the right to use the water of the Barberine and to turn the plateau into a storage lake of 39 million m³. The Barberine dam opened in 1925. Its water drove the power stations of Châtelard and Vernayaz.

Electricity use kept growing. In 1963 Switzerland and France signed a treaty for a new, larger scheme; it came into force in 1964. The Emosson dam was built further down from 1967 to 1974. The border was moved so that the dam lies fully in Switzerland. The new lake covered the old Barberine dam.
gained: The Emosson lake holds 227 million m³ of water. Two power plants have 200 MW and 190 MW. The SBB still use part of the water for railway electricity at Châtelard.
Together with the Vieux-Emosson lake and the Nant de Drance plant, the lakes now work as pumped storage. Water is pumped up when there is too much electricity and used again when demand is high.
lost: The lake covers the Barberine plateau. The map of 1920 shows the hamlet of Barberine, a club hut and the huts of Emosson there.
The old Barberine dam of 1925 now lies under the Emosson lake. Its top appears only when the water is low in spring.
Under the concession, water caught in France, in the upper basins of the Arve, the Giffre and the Eau Noire, is led into the lake. This water is taken from those streams.

title: Aare at the Grimsel (Grimselsee reservoir)
place: Upper Aare valley below the Unteraar glacier, at the Grimsel Pass
summary: Two dams at the Grimsel made one of the first large reservoirs of the Alps; the lake drowned the old Grimsel hospice and the valley floor of the young Aare.
why: Below the Unteraar glacier the young Aare flowed through a flat, stony valley floor. Near its end stood the old Grimsel hospice (Spittel), an inn for travellers that had belonged to the Hasli valley since the Middle Ages.

The canton gave the water rights in 1907. In 1925 the Kraftwerke Oberhasli (KWO) company was founded. From 1926 to 1932 it built the 114 m high Spitallamm dam in the gorge. A second dam, the 42 m high Seeuferegg dam, closes the lake towards the pass. The lake stores summer water for the power stations lower down the valley.
The concrete of the Spitallamm dam aged. A new arch dam was built just in front of it and finished in 2025. The old dam stays in place under the water.
gained: The lake stores about 94 million m³ of usable water. It is the main reservoir of the Oberhasli power plants.
The power plants brought wealth to the commune of Guttannen. The KWO is today the most important employer there.
lost: The old Grimsel hospice was flooded, together with parts of the old pass path.
The maps of 1924 and today show that the lake covered the valley floor of the Aare and two small natural lakes near the hospice.
With the new wages, farming in Guttannen became a side job.

title: Dixence (Lac des Dix, Grande Dixence dam)
place: Val des Dix, upper Val d'Hérémence (commune of Hérémence)
summary: Two dams turned the high Val des Dix into a reservoir; the Grande Dixence wall of 1961 is the highest gravity dam in the world.
why: The Val des Dix is a high valley above Hérémence. Before the dams, the Dixence flowed over a wide gravel bed with many arms. The map of 1928 shows summer pastures (alps) with huts on the valley floor.

The power company Energie Ouest Suisse (EOS) built a first dam here from 1929 to 1935. After 1945, electricity use grew fast and people wanted more power in winter. Grande Dixence SA was founded in 1950 and built a new, much higher wall further down from 1950 to 1961. It is a gravity dam (a dam that holds the water by its own weight). It is 285 m high.

More than 3,000 people worked on the site, in all weather, at about 2,400 m. The new lake covered the first dam. About 100 km of tunnels and pumping stations bring water from 35 glaciers into the lake. Since 1945 there was more and more opposition to dams, mainly for nature reasons.
gained: The lake holds about 400 million m³ of water. The plants make about 2 billion kWh of electricity per year on average, for the supply of 18 cantons.
The Cleuson-Dixence project (1993–1998) made the production capacity 2.5 times larger.
The HLS (Historical Dictionary of Switzerland) calls the dam a centre of tourism in the Valais, with visits to the dam.
lost: The lake covers the valley floor of the Val des Dix. The map of 1928 shows the alps of La Barma, Lautaret, Liappey and Cheilon there, with huts near the river.
The first Dixence dam (1929–1935) went out of service in 1957 and now lies under the lake.

The water intakes take water from the Borgne streams of the Val d'Hérens. In 2018 the canton ordered Grande Dixence SA to release minimum flows into the Borgne de Ferpècle and Borgne d'Arolla and to restore floodplains at Lotrey and Les Salays.

title: Lago Maggiore regulated by the Miorina weir
place: Lago Maggiore; weir on the Ticino below Sesto Calende (Italy)
summary: Since 1943 the Miorina weir on the Ticino in Italy controls the level of Lago Maggiore, mainly to store water for farms and power stations downstream.
why: Lago Maggiore is large, but its catchment (the area that drains into it) is about 30 times larger. After long rain the lake rises fast, sometimes far above the flood limit at Locarno.

People in Lombardy and Piedmont wanted a steady supply of water from the lake. Studies for a weir began in the 19th century. The Miorina weir was built from 1938 to 1942, about 3 km below the outflow at Sesto Calende. It started work on 1 January 1943.

The weir is about 200 m wide and has 120 metal gates. An Italian consortium of irrigation boards and the power company ENEL operates it. In summer the upper limit was raised by 25 cm in 2015 and by another 10 cm in 2019, as a test.
gained: The lake stores water for more than 7000 farms and 5 hydropower stations below the weir, and for shipping and tourism on the lake.
When the lake reaches the upper limit, all gates must open. This helps to protect the shores from floods.
lost: The weir cannot stop all floods, because the outflow at Sesto Calende is too small. In 2000 the lake reached its highest level since 1943 at Locarno.
When the gates are laid down at high water, they can only be raised again after the lake has fallen. So the weir has little control during a flood.

title: Drainage of the Linth plain (Linthebene melioration)
place: Linth plain between Lake Zurich, Uznach, Tuggen, Benken and Lake Walen
summary: From 1941 to 1964, as part of the wartime 'cultivation battle', the wet Riet land of the Linth plain was drained with canals, pipes and pumps, and 27.65 km² became farmland.
why: The Linth correction of 1807–1827 ended the big floods and the malaria. But the plain was never fully drained. Large areas stayed Riet (wet meadows with sedges and reeds), used for litter (dry plants as bedding in stables).

After the food shortage of the First World War, a project of 1918 failed. Unemployment in the 1930s and the 'cultivation battle' of the Second World War (the Wahlen plan, to grow more food at home) gave the push. A federal law of 1939 came into force in 1940. Work started in autumn 1941; interned Polish soldiers helped.

The works drained 2765 ha with 154 km of canals and concrete pipes and four pump stations. The ground water was lowered below the level of the Linth and Lake Zurich. Only a few Riet areas were left out, such as the reserve of the Swiss nature protection league in the Kaltbrunner Riet.
gained: About 27.65 km² of wet land became fields, more than the area of Lake Walen. The first 50 ha were farmed already in summer 1942.
Land consolidation (joining small plots into larger ones) covered more than 50 km². More than 150 km of new roads and paths cross the new farmland.
Work for unemployed people and more home-grown food in the war years.
lost: The wide wet Riet land of the plain became farmland. The landscape changed very fast.
The drained soil sank, most of all where the soil is peat and where maize is grown. The fields now depend on pumps.
The remaining Kaltbrunner Riet now lies higher than the fields around it. At the end of the 1970s it dried out and must now be watered artificially.

title: Saane (Lac de la Gruyère reservoir, Rossens dam)
place: Saane valley between Broc and Rossens
summary: The Rossens arch dam turned the Saane valley between Broc and Rossens into the Lac de la Gruyère, an artificial lake; the hamlet of Pont-en-Ogoz went under water.

The lake holds 200 million m³, covers up to 10 km² and reaches 677 m. There were conflicts between the people of the valley, the Fribourg power company and tourism. They became smaller over time.
gained: The water drives the Hauterive power station. It makes on average 280 million kWh of electricity per year.
lost: The hamlet of Pont-en-Ogoz was drowned. Only the ruins of its castle stand out of the water, on an island.
The lake covers the Saane valley between Broc and Rossens, with its gravel banks. The map of 1947 shows the wide gravel bed between Broc and Corbières.

title: Salanfe (Lac de Salanfe)
place: Plan de Salanfe below the Dents du Midi (commune of Evionnaz)
summary: A gravity dam turned the alpine plain of Salanfe below the Dents du Midi into a reservoir; the limestone rock lets water escape.
why: Below the Dents du Midi lies a flat high plain, the Plan de Salanfe. Streams from the mountains spread over it and joined at its east end. The map of 1946 shows alp huts at its edge.

Salanfe SA was founded in 1947. The power company EOS and the chemical company Lonza each held half of it. A gravity dam 52 m high was built at the outlet of the plain from 1947 to 1953. The first turbine at Miéville in the Rhône valley started on 30 December 1950.
The rock around the lake is partly limestone with cracks. From 1991 to 1994 cement was injected into the permeable zones, to make a watertight layer 600 m long.
gained: The lake holds 40 million m³ of water. The Miéville power station has an installed power of 70 to 80 MW.
Galleries and pumping stations bring water from the Saufla basin on the other side of the Tour Sallière into the lake.
lost: The lake covers most of the flat Plan de Salanfe. The map of 1946 shows streams spreading over the plain and alp huts at its north edge.
The water of the Salanfe basin and of the Saufla basin is caught and led to the Miéville power station.

title: Drize in the Praille-Acacias-Vernets quarter
place: Carouge, Lancy and Geneva: La Praille and the Praille-Acacias-Vernets (PAV) quarter
built: underground between 1950 and 1960 (maps); opened again 2023–2025 (first stage)
summary: The lower Drize across La Praille disappeared under a railway and industrial zone in the 1950s; since November 2025 it flows open again on 450 m in the new PAV quarter.
why: The Drize comes from the foot of the Salève and flows through Troinex and Carouge. On the map of 1950 its last stretch still ran open across the fields of La Praille to the Aire.
On the map of 1960 this stretch is gone. A railway yard and an industrial zone now cover La Praille. The Drize was led through an underground gallery below the route des Jeunes.

Geneva now builds a new quarter, Praille-Acacias-Vernets (PAV). The canton wants the Drize open again over 2.5 km, from Grange-Collomb to the Arve. The first stage, 450 m at the Etoile and in the Acacias quarter, was opened in November 2025. The whole project will take about 20 years.
gained: Land over the old open course: the map of 1960 shows the railway yard and the industrial zone of La Praille there.
Since 2025: cool and green places for the new quarter, refuges for plants and animals, and better flood protection, says the canton.
lost: The open lower Drize across La Praille disappeared. The maps show it open in 1950 and gone in 1960. The water ran in an underground gallery.
The open stream cost money: the Grand Council voted 60 million francs for the project, 35 million of it for the first stage.

title: Julia (Lai da Marmorera reservoir)
place: Upper Surses (Oberhalbstein) valley between Bivio and Mulegns
summary: An earth dam on the Julia made the Lai da Marmorera for the city of Zurich; the old village of Marmorera went under water in 1954.
why: In the upper Surses valley the Julia river flowed through a flat valley floor. The farm village of Marmorera and the hamlet of Cresta stood there, with a church, a school, meadows and woods.

The city of Zurich needed more electricity. In 1948 the village assembly voted 24 to 2 and gave the concession to the electricity works of the city of Zurich (EWZ). Zurich voters approved the money in 1949. The dam was built from 1950 to 1954. The water drives a power station at Tinizong.

The dam is a 91 m high earth dam, made of local soil. HLS calls it the first earth dam of this kind in Europe. Since 1954 the old village has been under water. A new village was built on the slope above the lake.
gained: The lake stores about 62.6 million m³ of water for electricity for the city of Zurich.
The city of Zurich gave the new village a church. Families got payments higher than the market value of their land, if they voted yes.
lost: The water covered the church, the school, 29 homes and 52 barns, the hamlet of Cresta and 140 ha of meadows and woods.
Some families were forcibly expropriated. Most moved to other villages in Graubünden. The village had 140 people in 1950 and only 28 in 1960.
In the new village above the lake no farmers live any more. The alpine pastures are rented to people from outside.

title: Doubs (Lac de Moron, Châtelot dam)
place: Doubs gorge on the French border below the Saut du Doubs (Les Brenets, Les Planchettes)
summary: A Franco-Swiss arch dam turned the Doubs gorge below the Saut du Doubs into the Lac de Moron; below it the river has very little water or strongly changing flows.
why: Below the Saut du Doubs waterfall the Doubs flows in a deep gorge. Here the river is the border between Switzerland and France. Mills had used its force on both sides since the 15th century.

The Société des Forces Motrices du Châtelot, with French and Swiss partners, built a concrete arch dam 74 m high from 1950 to 1953. Its lake is the Lac de Moron. The water goes through a tunnel to a power station about 4 km downstream.

The plant produces peak energy: it uses the water mainly when demand is high. This splits the Doubs into three parts: the lake, a stretch of 3.8 km below the dam with very little water, and a stretch below the power station with strong changes in flow.
gained: The power station has 30 MW and makes on average 100 GWh per year.
The lake holds 20 million m³ and covers 0.64 km².
lost: The Doubs below the Saut du Doubs became a lake, the Lac de Moron. The maps of 1949 and 1956 show the lake filling the gorge from the dam back to the Saut du Doubs.

Between the dam and the power station the Doubs keeps only 250 litres per second (the concession asked only 50 l/s). The Doubs plan (Plan d'assainissement du Doubs) proposed raising this to 2,000 l/s.
Below the power station, the irregular use makes the flow rise and fall strongly. Banks dry out, and the bed is flooded and laid dry in turn.

title: Lake Zurich regulated by the Platzspitz weir
place: Limmat at the Platzspitz in Zurich, about 2 km below the lake outflow
summary: After the mill buildings in the Limmat were removed, a new regulating weir at the Platzspitz (1951) and a deeper river bed cut the normal changes of Lake Zurich from up to 2 m to about half a metre.
why: In the early 20th century the level of Lake Zurich still changed by up to 2 m. Near the shore this often caused floods. The main reason was the mill buildings in the city, which blocked the bed of the Limmat.

After decades of effort the mill buildings were removed completely. In the early 1950s a new regulating weir replaced the old needle weir at the Platzspitz. The river bed above it was dug deeper. Since 1977 rules of the cantons Zurich, Schwyz, St. Gallen and Aargau set the lake level and the outflow for every day of the year.
gained: More water can leave the lake. The normal changes of the lake level fell to about half a metre, and shore floods became rarer.
When the Sihl brings a flood, the weir can hold back lake water for a short time, to protect the Limmat valley below Zurich.
lost: The old mill buildings in the Limmat in the city were removed, because they blocked the outflow of the lake.
The weir has limits: the floods of 1999 and 2005 showed that it cannot handle every event.

title: Valser Rhein (Zervreilasee reservoir)
place: Zervreila, upper Vals valley (Valsertal)
summary: A 151 m high arch dam closed the upper Vals valley; the Zervreilasee drowned the summer hamlets of Under and Ober Boda.
why: Above Vals, at about 1750 m, the Valser Rhein and the Canalbach met on a flat alpine valley floor. Zervreila had been a village, but people stopped living there all year in the 18th century. The farmers of Vals used the place for their cattle in summer.

From 1951 to 1958 the Kraftwerke Zervreila company built the power plants. The arch dam was built from 1953 to 1957. The lake is a seasonal store: it keeps summer water for winter. A tunnel takes the water from the Vals valley into the Safien valley, to power stations at Safien and Rothenbrunnen.
gained: The lake holds about 100 million m³ of water. Three power stations below it use the water, with a total installed power of about 230 MW.
lost: The water covered the two hamlets of Under Boda and Ober Boda and the alpine valley floor at Zervreila.
Much of the water now leaves the Vals valley through a tunnel to the Safien valley.

title: Drance de Bagnes (Lac de Mauvoisin)
place: Upper Val de Bagnes, below the Giétro glacier (commune of Bagnes)
summary: An arch dam closed the upper Val de Bagnes in 1957; its lake now fills the valley where the Giétro glacier once dammed the river and caused the flood of 1818.
why: In the upper Val de Bagnes the Drance flowed through a narrow valley below the Giétro glacier. Ice from this glacier sometimes blocked the river and a lake formed behind it. On 16 June 1818 the ice dam broke. About 20 million m³ of water emptied in about 30 minutes. The wave reached Martigny after about 90 minutes and killed 34 people. An earlier outburst in 1595 killed 140 people.

After 1945 electricity use grew fast. Forces Motrices de Mauvoisin SA built an arch dam (a thin curved wall that pushes the water load into the rock) at the mouth of the gorge from 1951 to 1957. The local museum says more than 1,800 men worked on the site every day between 1948 and 1958.
In 1989–1991 the wall was raised by 13.5 m to 250 m. The aim was to move more summer water into winter production.
gained: The lake holds 211.5 million m³ of water. It drives the power stations of Fionnay (127.5 MW) and Riddes (225 MW).
The raised wall (1991) lets the company store more summer water for winter electricity.
lost: The lake covers the valley floor of the Drance above the dam. The map of 1950 shows a path up the valley along the river there.
The dam holds back gravel. A study of the 1818 flood says the bed of the Drance below has probably risen since the dam was built, because the river now carries less material.
The dam and mass tourism changed the commune of Bagnes in the middle of the 20th century. Services replaced farming as the main work.

title: Rhine at Rheinau (Rheinau power plant)
place: Rhine loop at Rheinau, below the Rhine Falls
summary: A power plant on the Rhine loop at Rheinau caused one of the first big landscape fights in Switzerland; the river above it became calmer and the loop got less water.
why: Below the Rhine Falls the Rhine makes a tight loop around the old monastery of Rheinau. In 1944 and 1947 Switzerland and the German district office of Waldshut gave the licence for a power plant here. The plant may use up to 400 m³/s of Rhine water.

Nature and heritage groups protested. They said the water would back up into the basin of the Rhine Falls. They also said the works would harm the landscape. With the Rheinau initiative they forced a stop of the building work. In 1954 the Swiss voters clearly rejected the initiative. Only the canton of Schaffhausen voted yes. The village of Rheinau itself was split by the fight. The plant started work in 1956.
The fight helped to change the law. After the initiatives of the 1950s, the voters added an article on nature and heritage protection to the federal constitution in 1962.
gained: The plant makes electricity for Switzerland and Germany. Zurich has 53.6%, Baden-Württemberg 38.3% and Schaffhausen 8.1% of the water power.
The protest led to stronger protection of nature and landscape in the Swiss constitution (1962).
lost: The river above the weir became a calm, held-back stretch. HLS says living conditions changed in such reservoirs with weak current.

The river loop at Rheinau became a residual water stretch. This is a river part that gets only the water the power plant leaves. By law it must be improved; in 2011 the authorities were still deciding how.

title: Lienne (Lac de Tseuzier)
place: Upper Lienne valley below the Rawil pass, north of Sion
summary: An arch dam made a lake on the Rawil alp in 1957; in 1978 a test tunnel for a motorway drained the rock and damaged the dam.
why: Below the Rawil pass the Lienne flowed over a flat alp, the Montagne du Rawil. Electricité de la Lienne SA built an arch dam 156 m high at the narrow exit of this basin from 1954 to 1957. The water goes to power stations lower down, at St-Léonard in the Rhône valley.

In the last months of 1978, measurements showed unusual movements of the dam. The rock below had sunk by 13 cm, and the two sides of the valley had moved 7 to 8 cm closer together. The cause was the test tunnel (galerie de sondage) for a planned motorway tunnel under the Rawil. The tunnel drained water from the cracked rock, and the ground sank like a bowl 2 to 3 km wide.

The dam was badly damaged and could not work normally for a long time. It was repaired from 1982 to 1984. The federal offices later used this case to watch dams near the new Gotthard and Lötschberg base tunnels.
gained: The lake holds 12.6 million m³ of water. The power plants of the scheme have 100 MW in total.
The damage of 1978 taught engineers how tunnels can move dams. Since 1992 the federal offices have required close monitoring of dams near the AlpTransit tunnels.
lost: The lake covers the flat floor of the Rawil alp. The map of 1953 shows the stream winding over this alp, with a few buildings.
In 1978 the drained rock damaged the dam. Normal use was impossible for a long time.

title: Gougra (Lac de Moiry)
place: Val de Moiry above Grimentz, Val d'Anniviers
summary: An arch-gravity dam above Grimentz turned the alp of Moiry into a reservoir for the power plants of the Val d'Anniviers.
why: Above Grimentz the Gougra flowed through the high Val de Moiry. The valley floor was a summer pasture (alp) with huts, the Alpe de Moiry.

After 1945 electricity use grew fast. Forces Motrices de la Gougra SA built a dam 148 m high at the end of the alp from 1954 to 1958. It is an arch-gravity dam (a curved wall that is also heavy). The water drives three power stations: Mottec, Vissoie and Chippis.
The scheme also uses water from the Turtmann valley next to it.
gained: The lake holds 77 million m³ of water. The plants have 168 MW and make on average 643 GWh of electricity per year.
The water passes three power stations on its way down: Mottec, Vissoie and Chippis.
lost: The lake covers the floor of the Val de Moiry. The map of 1953 shows the Gougra winding over the Alpe de Moiry, with alp huts and paths.
Water from the Gougra and from the Turtmann valley is taken into the scheme.

title: Maggia (Lago del Sambuco)
place: Val Sambuco above Fusio, top of the Valle Maggia (Lavizzara)
summary: An arch-gravity dam above Fusio stores the water of the upper Maggia; below it, the river has carried little water ever since.
why: Above Fusio the young Maggia flowed through the Val Sambuco. The valley floor had the alp of Sambuco with many buildings.
The power company Ofima built an arch-gravity dam 130 m high from 1954 to 1956. The lake stores water for the power stations of Peccia, Cavergno and Verbano further down the valley.

Below the intakes the Maggia keeps only little water. In 2019 the Ticino parliament passed a law on minimum flows (the least water that must stay in a river). Ofima and Ofible went to court, and in April 2022 the cantonal court decided in their favour.
gained: The lake holds 64 million m³ of water. It feeds a chain of power stations with 48 MW (Peccia), 104 MW (Cavergno) and 106 MW (Verbano).
lost: The lake covers the Val Sambuco. The map of 1953 shows the alp of Sambuco with many buildings on the valley floor.
Pro Natura, WWF and the fishing federation call the remaining flows of the Maggia scarce. They say the low water warms up too much in summer and has harmed the fish.
In 2019 the Ticino parliament passed a law on minimum flows. After the court decision of April 2022, RSI reports that Ticino has no minimum flows.

title: Göschener Reuss (Göscheneralpsee reservoir)
place: Göscheneralp, upper Göschenen valley above Göschenen
summary: An earth dam closed the upper Göschenen valley; the reservoir drowned the farm hamlet of Göscheneralp to make electricity for the railways and central Switzerland.
why: At the end of the Göschenen valley lay a flat valley floor at about 1710 m. The Göschener Reuss wound through it. The families of the hamlet Göscheneralp lived only from farming. They used about 45 ha of hay meadows on the valley floor.

The power companies first wanted to flood the Urseren valley near Andermatt. Strong protest stopped that plan in 1951. The Göschenen power plant was built as a smaller replacement. The SBB (Swiss Federal Railways) and the CKW (Central Swiss power company) built it together from 1955 to 1962.

The dam is a 155 m high earth and rock dam. All households in the hamlet had to leave. According to a study from 1963, the land was sold without forced expropriation. The avalanche winter of 1951 had made some people more willing to sell.
gained: The reservoir holds about 75 million m³ of water. In 1963 the plant was expected to make 320 GWh per year, 137 GWh of it in winter.
Half of the electricity goes to the railway network, the other half to the CKW grid.
Seven men from the resettled families got jobs with the power company, as workers and as road and water wardens.
lost: The water covered the hamlet Göscheneralp and the meadows of the valley floor. In the hamlet, 7 land owners with 37 people were affected.
In all, the company bought land from 11 owners with 60 people, in Göscheneralp and Gwüest. This included 10 houses, 28 stables, an inn, a hotel, a chapel and a school house.
The remaining families got new houses in Gwüest below the dam. A new chapel and school were built there.

title: Reno di Lei (Lago di Lei reservoir)
place: Valle di Lei, an Italian valley south of Innerferrera; the dam stands on Swiss ground
summary: A 138 m high dam closed the Valle di Lei; the lake lies almost all in Italy, and the two countries swapped land so that the dam stands in Switzerland.
why: The Valle di Lei is a high valley on the border, open to the north towards the Swiss valley of Ferrera. Farmers used it as alpine pasture for their cattle, with small alp buildings on the valley floor.

After the Rheinwald valley had refused a huge reservoir, the Kraftwerke Hinterrhein (KHR) chose the Valle di Lei for their main lake. Work began in summer 1957. The lake was full for the first time in autumn 1962. Italy has a share in the company.

The dam was first on Italian ground. After it was finished, Switzerland and Italy exchanged land in 1962-63. About 45 ha of the valley came to the Swiss commune of Innerferrera, so the dam now stands on Swiss ground.
gained: The lake holds about 197 million m³ of water. It is the heart of the Hinterrhein power plants, which make on average about 1500 GWh of electricity per year.
About two thirds of its water comes through tunnels from the Avers, Madris and Niemet valleys.
lost: The lake covered the valley floor of the Reno di Lei, which was used as alpine pasture. The map of 1956 shows alp buildings such as Alpe Rebella, Rossi Nuovi and Rossi Vecchi beside the river.
Water from the Avers, Madris and Niemet valleys is taken away from their streams and led into the lake.

title: Limmernbach (Limmerensee reservoir)
place: Limmernboden, a high valley south-west of Linthal, above Tierfehd
summary: A 146 m high arch dam closed the Limmernboden above Linthal; the reservoir filled the flat stony floor of this high valley.
why: The Limmernboden lies above Tierfehd, at the end of the Linth valley. It is a flat, stony high valley at about 1750 m, with steep walls. Several streams wound across it.

From 1957 to 1965 the Kraftwerke Linth-Limmern company built a high-pressure storage power system. The 146 m high Limmernboden arch dam closes the valley. The water falls more than 1000 m to the power station at Tierfehd and is used again further down at Linthal.
gained: HLS calls the plant of national importance. It brought about 40 jobs, tax income for Linthal and water fees for the local communities (Tagwen).
The lake holds about 92 million m³ of water. The Tierfehd power station alone has 261 MW.
lost: The maps of 1957 and today show that the lake covered the flat floor of the Limmernboden with its braided streams.

title: Hinterrhein (Sufnersee reservoir)
place: Valley floor below the village of Sufers, Rheinwald
summary: A dam in the gorge below Sufers made a reservoir on the Hinterrhein; it drowned about 30 ha of meadows, after the valley had stopped a much larger lake.
why: From 1942 the power companies planned a huge reservoir of 280 million m³ in the Rheinwald valley. It would have flooded most of the valley, including the village of Splügen. From 1940 to 1944 the people of the Rheinwald fought the plan. Splügen, Medels and Nufenen refused the water rights, and the plan was dropped.

Instead, the Kraftwerke Hinterrhein company (founded in 1956) built the large Valle di Lei reservoir and a smaller lake at Sufers. The Sufers reservoir was built from 1959 to 1962. It evens out the river flow, which changes a lot with rain and snow melt. Water can also be pumped from it up to the Valle di Lei.
gained: The lake has a usable volume of about 16 million m³. It is part of the Hinterrhein power plants, which make on average about 1500 GWh of electricity per year.
The valley kept its villages: the much larger Rheinwald reservoir, which would have drowned Splügen, was not built.
lost: The lake covered about 30 ha of meadows on the valley floor. This was almost 20% of all the hay harvest of the commune.

title: Lago di Lugano regulated at Ponte Tresa
place: Outflow of the Tresa from Lago di Lugano at Ponte Tresa (border Switzerland–Italy)
summary: Since 1963 a weir on the Tresa at Ponte Tresa, built under a Swiss–Italian agreement of 1955, regulates the level of Lago di Lugano.
why: People spoke about regulating Lago di Lugano already in 1795. About a hundred years later they began to study how to lower the lake at high water and how to use the water power of the Tresa. Talks between Italy and Switzerland took place from 1910 to 1913, then stopped.

Talks started again in 1951. On 17 September 1955 the two countries signed an agreement in Lugano. Building began in 1960, and the weir started work in 1963. It lies about 300 m below the lake outflow and has three flaps, each 14 m long. The canton of Ticino operates it.
gained: High lake levels are reduced, and the maximum flow of the Tresa is limited. This reduces the flood risk along the Tresa.
At low water the weir lets out more water, so that the Creva power station on the Tresa can work.
The level is set with regard to farming, fishing, shipping and tourism.
lost: The outflow is no longer natural. A fixed set of rules gives the outflow for each day of the year and each lake level.
The weir cannot stop all floods. In 2002 the lake reached its highest level since 1963.

Space for the city's sewage plant, sports buildings and today a lakeside park and beach.

title: Saaser Vispa (Mattmark reservoir)
place: Mattmark plain at the head of the Saas valley (Saas-Almagell)
summary: An earth dam closed the Mattmark plain below the Allalin glacier; during the work, an ice avalanche killed 88 workers in 1965.
why: At the head of the Saas valley the Saaser Vispa flowed over a flat plain of gravel, the Mattmark plain. In the past the Allalin glacier sometimes reached the valley floor and blocked the river. A paper of 1957 says the Mattmark lake behind the ice burst about thirty times in four hundred years. The largest floods came in 1633, 1772 and 1834.

After 1945 electricity use grew fast. Kraftwerke Mattmark AG built an earth dam (a dam made of piled rock and moraine material with a watertight core) from 1960 to 1967. It is 117 m high. The water drives power stations at Zermeiggern and Stalden.

On 30 August 1965 about two million m³ of ice and rock broke off the Allalin glacier. It buried the barracks, workshops and canteen of the building site. 88 people died: 56 Italians, 23 Swiss, 4 Spaniards, 2 Germans, 2 Austrians and 1 stateless person. In 1972 the courts acquitted all 17 people charged.
gained: The lake holds 100 million m³ of usable water. The two power stations below have 74 MW and 185 MW.
In 2001 the flood spillway was changed for flood protection.
lost: 88 people died in the ice avalanche of 1965, most of them Italian guest workers. 11 were injured.
The lake covers the Mattmark plain. The map of 1959 shows a hotel and the Distelalp with its huts there, near the path to the Monte Moro pass.
For the compensation basin below the dam, the hamlet of Zer Meiggeru (Zermeiggern) with its chapel of 1707 had to give way in 1961.

title: Brenno di Luzzone (Lago di Luzzone)
place: Val di Luzzone above Ghirone, upper Valle di Blenio
summary: An arch dam closed the Val di Luzzone above Ghirone in 1963 and stores summer water of the upper Blenio valley for winter.
why: Above Ghirone the Brenno di Luzzone flowed through a side valley with alps and the small hamlet of Cavallo. The land belonged to the patriziati (old community corporations) of Ghirone and Aquila.

The power company Ofible built an arch dam here from 1960 to 1963. A new road and the Toira tunnel were opened in 1958 for the building site. During the work the population of Ghirone rose to 340 in 1960. The water comes from the area between the Lucomagno pass and the Adula.
From 1995 to 1999 the wall was raised by 17 m, from 208 m to 225 m. This added 20 million m³ of storage for more winter production.
gained: The lake holds 107 million m³. Of the 130 million m³ that flow in during summer on average, 107 million can be kept for winter, when demand is highest.
The full lake is an energy reserve of about 240 GWh.
The new road and the Toira tunnel (1958) were built for the dam. With a ski lift (1964), they strongly helped summer and winter tourism in Campo, says the HLS.
lost: The lake covers the floor of the Val di Luzzone. The map of 1959 shows the hamlet of Cavallo and alp buildings at Al Sasso there, now under water.
Water of the upper Blenio valley that flows in during summer is stored in the lake and used in winter.
